name: Kenzo Tange
bio: Born in Osaka in 1913 and raised in provincial Imabari, Tange discovered Le Corbusier in a magazine as an indifferent student and decided architecture was worth being serious about. Winning the 1949 competition for Hiroshima's Peace Park gave the atomized city its civic center and gave Japan a modernism that could carry national grief. From his laboratory at the University of Tokyo — through which Maki, Isozaki, Kurokawa and Taniguchi all passed — he floated the 1960 Plan for Tokyo, a city extended on megastructures across its own bay, and effectively fathered Metabolism without joining it. The paired gymnasia at Yoyogi, suspension roofs swung between temple silhouette and engineering feat, remain the great architectural image of the 1964 Olympics. He won the Pritzker in 1987, rebuilt half of downtown Tokyo in his corporate late phase, and was given his funeral in his own St. Mary's Cathedral.

projects.title: Yoyogi National Gymnasium
projects.blurb: Two suspension-roofed arenas for the 1964 Olympics — cables engineered like a bridge, profiles pitched like temple roofs.

projects.title: Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park
projects.blurb: The competition win that defined postwar Japanese modernism: museum, axis and cenotaph aligned on the ruined dome.

projects.title: St. Mary's Cathedral
projects.blurb: Eight hyperbolic-paraboloid shells in stainless steel rising from a cruciform of light; Tange's funeral was held here.

projects.title: Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building
projects.blurb: Twin towers splitting like a Gothic cathedral rewired with circuit-board facades — the bubble era's city hall.

projects.title: Kagawa Prefectural Government Office
projects.blurb: Concrete post-and-beam handled like temple carpentry; the building that reconciled modernism with Japanese tradition.

projects.title: Yamanashi Press and Broadcasting Centre
projects.blurb: Sixteen service shafts with floors plugged in between — Metabolist theory actually built, extensions left waiting.

projects.title: Plan for Tokyo 1960
projects.blurb: The unbuilt megastructural city stretched across Tokyo Bay on a spine of loops; the most influential drawing of the Metabolist decade.

projects.title: Kurashiki City Hall
projects.blurb: Stacked concrete beams like a log storehouse monumentalized; now the city art museum.

projects.title: Shizuoka Press and Broadcasting Center
projects.blurb: A tiny Metabolist tower on a traffic island in Ginza — capsules clipped to a single cylindrical core.

projects.title: Fuji Television Building
projects.blurb: A gridded frame in Odaiba with a titanium sphere caught in it; the late corporate Tange at his most emblematic.

name: Lina Bo Bardi
bio: Born in Rome and trained in the wreckage of wartime Milan, Bo Bardi sailed for Brazil in 1946 and decided almost immediately that she had found her country. She fused rough concrete with the popular culture of the Brazilian northeast, collected folk objects as seriously as she read Gramsci, and argued that buildings belong to the people who use them rather than the critics who photograph them. MASP lifted an art museum off the ground to give São Paulo a public plaza; SESC Pompéia turned a factory into a working-class palace of leisure. Long under-recognized outside Brazil, she is now read as one of the century's essential architects — and one of its best writers on what architecture is for.

projects.title: MASP
projects.blurb: An art museum hung from two red beams, leaving the ground free as a public plaza.

projects.title: SESC Pompéia
projects.blurb: A factory turned leisure center, with sports towers linked by aerial walkways.

projects.title: Casa de Vidro
projects.blurb: Her own glass house on slender pilotis, now swallowed by the forest it planted.

projects.title: Solar do Unhão
projects.blurb: A sugar estate restored around a sculptural wooden stair; home of Bahia's Museum of Modern Art.
projects.wikipedia: Museum of Modern Art of Bahia

projects.title: Teatro Oficina
projects.blurb: A theater as street — scaffolding seats along a raw open spine.

projects.title: Igreja Espírito Santo do Cerrado
projects.blurb: A humble church built with the community that would use it.

projects.title: Casa do Benin
projects.blurb: A cultural house linking Bahia to West Africa.

projects.title: Ladeira da Misericórdia
projects.blurb: Prototype for rebuilding a crumbling historic hillside.

projects.title: Chame-Chame House
projects.blurb: A curved house grown around a jackfruit tree (demolished).

projects.title: Valéria Cirell House
projects.blurb: A rustic counterpoint to the Glass House, clad in pebbles and plants.

name: Eladio Dieste
bio: Dieste was an engineer, not an architect, and never stopped pointing that out; the buildings simply refused to stay on the engineering shelf. Born in Artigas in 1917 to Galician emigrants — the poet Rafael Dieste was his uncle — he invented cerámica armada, thin shells of ordinary brick laced with steel and posed in double curvature, because concrete was expensive in Uruguay and brick was not. With the firm Dieste y Montañez he applied it mostly to unglamorous programs: grain silos, fruit-packing sheds, bus terminals, wool warehouses, all built cheaply and still standing. Twice, at Atlántida and Durazno, the method rose to church-building, and the undulating walls of Cristo Obrero — now a World Heritage Site — are among the most moving religious spaces of the century. He insisted that economy was a moral question and that there is a resistant virtue in form itself; almost nothing he built has needed rescue since.

projects.title: Church of Christ the Worker
projects.blurb: Walls and roof that undulate for stiffness, all in bare brick; a rural parish church now on the World Heritage list.
projects.wikipedia: Iglesia de Cristo Obrero y Nuestra Señora de Lourdes

projects.title: Church of San Pedro
projects.blurb: A fire-gutted 19th-century church rebuilt with a folded brick facade and a floating rose window of voids.

projects.title: Salto Municipal Bus Terminal
projects.blurb: Long-span Gaussian brick vaults sheltering provincial buses — infrastructure treated with cathedral care.

projects.title: Julio Herrera y Obes Warehouse
projects.blurb: Port storage under self-supporting double-curved vaults; the masterpiece nobody visits.

projects.title: Cítricos Caputto Packing Plant
projects.blurb: Fruit sheds spanned by free-standing brick shells — cheaper than steel, and better looking.

projects.title: TEM Factory
projects.blurb: An early industrial hall where the Gaussian vault system was worked out at full scale.

projects.title: Montevideo Shopping Center
projects.blurb: A shopping mall under his brick vaults; commerce granted the same structural dignity as worship.

projects.title: Cadyl Horizontal Silo
projects.blurb: A grain silo as a single self-supporting brick tube; agricultural engineering at its most elegant.

projects.title: Salto Gymnasium
projects.blurb: A municipal sports hall vaulted in reinforced ceramics, span held by curvature alone.

projects.title: Lanera Uruguaya Warehouse
projects.blurb: Wool storage under sinuous shells; late proof the system worked at any scale the client could afford.

name: I. M. Pei
firm: I. M. Pei & Partners / Pei Cobb Freed
bio: Born in Guangzhou in 1917 and raised partly in the classical gardens of Suzhou, the banker's son sailed for America at seventeen and never practiced anywhere else, though China kept calling him back. After MIT, Harvard under Gropius, and a decade as house architect to the developer William Zeckendorf — an apprenticeship in real estate that his refined peers considered slumming — he founded his own firm in 1955 and climbed steadily from slab housing to the Kennedy Library. His geometry was unfashionably pure: triangles and knife edges in concrete, stone and glass, executed with a perfectionism that made the East Building's sharpest corner shiny from visitors touching it. The Louvre pyramid, denounced across Paris in 1984, became the city's least regretted modern monument. He won the Pritzker in 1983, spent the prize money sending Chinese students to architecture school, and finished his late trio — Miho, Suzhou, Doha — well past eighty. He died in 2019 at 102.

projects.title: Louvre Pyramid
projects.blurb: A glass pyramid reorganizing the world's most visited museum from below; scandal on arrival, landmark within a decade.

projects.title: East Building, National Gallery of Art
projects.blurb: Two interlocking triangles cut from a trapezoidal site; its 19-degree marble corner is polished by decades of hands.

projects.title: Bank of China Tower
projects.blurb: A tower of diagonally braced glass prisms growing like bamboo — Hong Kong's skyline sharpened to a point.

projects.title: Museum of Islamic Art
projects.blurb: Stacked limestone volumes on an artificial island, distilled from the Ibn Tulun mosque; designed at ninety-one.

projects.title: Miho Museum
projects.blurb: A museum mostly buried in a mountain, reached through a tunnel and across a bridge — Shangri-La with climate control.

projects.title: John F. Kennedy Presidential Library
projects.blurb: The commission that made his name, chosen by Jacqueline Kennedy; a white geometry and a vast glass void of mourning.
projects.wikipedia: John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum

projects.title: Mesa Laboratory
projects.blurb: Atmospheric research towers in pink bush-hammered concrete, modeled on Anasazi cliff dwellings above the plains.

projects.title: Suzhou Museum
projects.blurb: A return, in whitewashed walls and grey trim, to the garden city of his childhood — his declared farewell to China.

projects.title: Dallas City Hall
projects.blurb: An inverted concrete wedge leaning 34 degrees over its plaza; civic monumentality as pure section.

projects.title: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame
projects.blurb: A glass tent and cantilevered drums on Lake Erie, by an architect who cheerfully admitted he had to be taught the music.
projects.wikipedia: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame

name: Paul Rudolph
bio: A Methodist preacher's son from Kentucky, Rudolph learned lightness in Sarasota — ingenious little beach houses with Ralph Twitchell — and structure in the Brooklyn Navy Yard, welding ship hulls through the war between Harvard semesters under Gropius. Appointed chair at Yale at thirty-nine, he built the Art and Architecture Building as a personal manifesto: thirty-seven levels in seven stories, corduroy concrete raked by hand to catch shadow. Foster and Rogers studied under him there; the building burned in 1969, the counterculture cheered, and brutalism's fall took Rudolph's American career down with it. He spent his last decades building towers in Asia while his buildings at home were neglected, threatened and mutilated. Since his death in 1997 the demolition fights over his work have made him modernism's favorite martyr, and the drawings — those perspective sections, hatched like engravings — have never left the syllabus.

projects.title: Yale Art and Architecture Building
projects.blurb: A pinwheel of interlocking levels in hand-hammered corduroy concrete; burned in 1969, restored as Rudolph Hall in 2008.

projects.title: Boston Government Service Center
projects.blurb: A swirling concrete acropolis of ribbed walls and rogue staircases — brutalism at full orchestra, never quite finished.

projects.title: Orange County Government Center
projects.blurb: Eighty-seven roofs in restless composition for county paperwork; partially demolished in 2015 after a decade of preservation war.

projects.title: Milam Residence
projects.blurb: A beach facade of pure rectangles arranged like a Mondrian in white block, framing the Atlantic.

projects.title: Healy Guest House
projects.blurb: The Cocoon House — a catenary roof sprayed with the Navy's mothballing plastic, hovering over a Sarasota bayou.

projects.title: Walker Guest House
projects.blurb: A pavilion rigged with red cannonball counterweights; its flaps open like a crab, as Rudolph said, or close like a cocoon.

projects.title: UMass Dartmouth Campus
projects.blurb: An entire university conceived as one continuous concrete megastructure — his largest built work.

projects.title: Tuskegee University Chapel
projects.blurb: A twisting brick sanctuary without right angles for the historically Black university, acoustics tuned for its choir.

projects.title: Lippo Centre
projects.blurb: Twin glass towers gripped by projecting bays — koalas climbing a tree, per the local nickname; late Rudolph gone vertical.

projects.title: 23 Beekman Place
projects.blurb: His own quadruplex penthouse, a steel labyrinth of floating floors and vertigo edges rebuilt over twenty years.

name: Jørn Utzon
bio: Son of a naval architect, Utzon grew up around hull drawings in Aalborg and absorbed his sense of form from boats, Mayan platforms and Chinese roofs as much as from the Danish academy. In 1957, at thirty-eight, his competition sketches for an opera house on Bennelong Point — reportedly rescued from the rejects by Eero Saarinen — won him Sydney; his spherical solution of 1961 turned the impossible shells into segments of one orange. A hostile new state government starved him of fees and authority, and in 1966 he left Australia, never returned, and never saw the finished building. He consoled himself with courtyard housing, a cliff house on Mallorca built of local sandstone, the cloud-vaulted concrete of Bagsværd, and a marble parliament for Kuwait. The Pritzker came in 2003, and Sydney entered the World Heritage list in 2007 while its architect, by then nearly blind, was still alive to hear of it.

projects.title: Sydney Opera House
projects.blurb: Shell vaults cut from a single imagined sphere over a granite platform; the century's most recognized building, finished by others after its architect walked away.

projects.title: Bagsværd Church
projects.blurb: A plain industrial exterior hiding billowing concrete clouds — light handled as generously as in any baroque nave.

projects.title: Kuwait National Assembly
projects.blurb: A parliament under a concrete canopy that sags like a bedouin tent toward the gulf.

projects.title: Can Lis
projects.blurb: His exile house on a Mallorcan cliff — rooms of golden sandstone aimed at the sea, furniture built into the stone.

projects.title: Kingo Houses
projects.blurb: Sixty L-shaped courtyard houses ringing a pond, packed like cells in a honeycomb; Danish housing at its most humane.

projects.title: Fredensborg Houses
projects.blurb: The Kingo idea refined for returning diplomats — yellow-brick courtyards stepping down a meadow.

projects.title: Utzon Center
projects.blurb: His last work, on his hometown harborfront where his father designed yachts — shipyard roofs over an architecture school.

projects.title: Paustian House
projects.blurb: A furniture showroom with a canopy of concrete beech trunks, columns branching like the forest edge.

projects.title: Can Feliz
projects.blurb: The second Mallorca house, higher in the hills when Can Lis proved too exposed; his own definition of paradise.

projects.title: Melli Bank
projects.blurb: A bank hall for Tehran lit through a vaulted ceiling of suspended elements — the little-known rehearsal for Bagsværd.

name: Geoffrey Bawa
bio: Bawa came to architecture late and sideways: born in Colombo in 1919 to a wealthy family of mixed Muslim and Burgher descent, he read English at Cambridge, qualified as a barrister, and drifted until an abandoned rubber estate at Lunuganga, bought in 1948, gave him something worth learning a profession for. Qualified at the AA at thirty-eight, he joined the old colonial firm of Edwards, Reid & Begg and quietly turned it into the laboratory of tropical modernism — deep verandahs, courtyards, long roofs, and no air-conditioned wall between building and garden. His hotels taught the Asian resort its entire vocabulary, a debt the industry has been repaying in imitation ever since; his parliament sits on an island in an artificial lake like a pavilioned citadel. A stroke silenced him in 1998, and he died in 2003; Lunuganga, the garden he edited for fifty years, remains his most complete work.

projects.title: Sri Lankan Parliament
projects.blurb: A parliament of copper-roofed pavilions on an island in an artificial lake — monumental without a single colonnade of bombast.

projects.title: Lunuganga
projects.blurb: The garden estate he composed for half a century, moving hills and framing views; the autobiography he never wrote.

projects.title: Kandalama Hotel
projects.blurb: A hotel pressed against a rock ridge and deliberately swallowed by jungle, its facade a trellis for the forest to climb.

projects.title: Number 11
projects.blurb: Four row houses on a lane, slowly annexed and fused into his own labyrinth of courtyards, corridors and borrowed light.

projects.title: Ena de Silva House
projects.blurb: The urban courtyard house that launched his mature manner; later dismantled and rebuilt brick by brick at Lunuganga.

projects.title: Seema Malaka
projects.blurb: A meditation temple floating on Beira Lake on three linked platforms.

projects.title: University of Ruhuna
projects.blurb: A campus of pavilions and loggias draped over two hills by the sea — his largest ensemble, walkable entirely under cover.

projects.title: Bentota Beach Hotel
projects.blurb: The prototype tropical resort, built on a moated mound with batik ceilings; the template a whole industry copied.

projects.title: Lighthouse Hotel
projects.blurb: A hotel braced against the monsoon surf on Galle's rocks, entered up a spiral stair wrapped in a sculpted colonial battle.

projects.title: Triton Hotel
projects.blurb: An axis of reflecting pools running straight through the lobby to the ocean — arrival staged as a single wet horizon.

name: Paolo Soleri
bio: Soleri took a doctorate in Turin, apprenticed at Taliesin West in 1947, and lasted about eighteen months before Wright and he agreed they did not need each other. He stayed in the desert, built the half-buried Dome House at thirty, detoured home to Italy for a ceramics factory that spirals down a cliff, then settled at Paradise Valley and began casting structures from the earth itself, financed by the bronze windbells his foundation sells to this day. Arcology, his 1969 fusion of architecture and ecology, proposed hyperdense car-free megastructures as the alternative to sprawl, drawn on scrolls that filled museum walls. Arcosanti, the prototype begun in 1970 with volunteer labor in the high desert, remains perhaps five percent complete — less a failure than a very slow argument. He died in 2013; his daughter Daniela's 2017 account of his sexual abuse has since forced a harder accounting of the prophet, even as the cities he warned about keep sprawling on schedule.

projects.title: Arcosanti
projects.blurb: The prototype arcology rising in the Arizona high desert — vaults, apses and amphitheaters built by five decades of volunteers, permanently unfinished.

projects.title: Cosanti
projects.blurb: His home, studio and bell foundry of silt-cast concrete shells dug into a suburban lot; now an Arizona historic site.

projects.title: Dome House
projects.blurb: A desert house sunk into rock under a rotating glass dome, designed with Mark Mills; passive solar before the term existed.

projects.title: Ceramica Artistica Solimene
projects.blurb: A ceramics factory on the Amalfi coast, its facade scaled like a fish with pottery, production spiraling down an internal ramp.

projects.title: Paolo Soleri Amphitheater
projects.blurb: An earth-cast outdoor theater at the Santa Fe Indian School, beloved by performers; demolished in 2024 after years of contention.

projects.title: Soleri Bridge and Plaza
projects.blurb: A pedestrian bridge doubling as a solar calendar — the only bridge built from his lifetime of bridge designs.

projects.title: Mesa City
projects.blurb: A theoretical desert city for two million, drawn over years on huge paper rolls; the rehearsal for arcology.

projects.title: Arcology: The City in the Image of Man
projects.blurb: The book of thirty visionary megastructure cities that made his name and lodged the arcology in science fiction's vocabulary.

projects.title: Earth House
projects.blurb: The first structure at Cosanti, cast against a mound of earth then excavated — the technique that built everything after.

projects.title: Glass and Ceramics Studios, Cosanti
projects.blurb: Workshop apses whose curved earth-cast roofs shade the craftsmen who fund the utopia, bell by bronze bell.

name: Gottfried Böhm
bio: Böhm was born in 1920 into a dynasty of church builders — his father Dominikus was Germany's great ecclesiastical modernist — and trained as a sculptor as well as an architect, which explains nearly everything he built. Taking over the family office in Cologne in 1955, with his architect wife Elisabeth as lifelong collaborator, he spent the sixties pouring churches and town halls as if concrete were clay: Neviges is a walk-in mountain range, Bensberg a crystalline keep grafted onto a medieval castle. When concrete fell from grace he shifted without apology to steel and glass, and his sons Stephan, Peter and Paul carried the office into a fourth generation. In 1986 he became the first German to win the Pritzker, an honor he received with visible suspicion of the fuss. He worked from the family house in Cologne-Marienburg into extreme old age and died in 2021 at 101.

projects.title: Neviges Pilgrimage Church
projects.blurb: A faceted concrete mountain for 6,000 pilgrims, its interior a cave of angled light — brutalism's great sacred space.

projects.title: Bensberg Town Hall
projects.blurb: A concrete castle keep grown out of medieval ruins, its stair tower spiraling to a sculpted crown.

projects.title: Madonna in the Ruins Chapel
projects.blurb: A small chapel built into the bombed shell of St. Kolumba around a surviving statue; his first work, later wrapped by Zumthor's museum.

projects.title: Church of the Resurrection
projects.blurb: A fortress-like parish church in raw concrete and red brick at Melaten, folded like a piece of origami in masonry.

projects.title: St. Gertrud
projects.blurb: A tent of crumpled concrete on a Cologne street corner — the family trade continued in his own jagged dialect.

projects.title: Züblin-Haus
projects.blurb: Headquarters for a construction firm: two office slabs of red precast concrete joined by a vast glass hall, his postmodern turn.

projects.title: Hans Otto Theater
projects.blurb: A lakeside theater under nested red shell roofs, built in his eighties; Niemeyer curves with a Brandenburg accent.

projects.title: Ulm Central Library
projects.blurb: A glass pyramid of reading rooms spiraling above the medieval market square.

projects.title: WDR Arkaden
projects.blurb: A broadcasting complex threaded through a city block behind glassy arcades — urban repair in his lighter late manner.

projects.title: Diocesan Museum
projects.blurb: A treasury museum hung inside a dark metallic shell beside the cathedral, its interior a stepped concrete landscape.

name: Alison & Peter Smithson
bio: Alison Gill and Peter Smithson met as architecture students in Newcastle, married in 1949, and the next year — she was twenty-one — won the competition for a school at Hunstanton whose exposed steel, brick and plumbing gave the New Brutalism its founding building and its name. They built remarkably little and argued remarkably much: through the Independent Group and the 1956 This Is Tomorrow exhibition, through Team 10, which they helped run and which finished off CIAM, and through a shelf of books that made ordinariness, the street and the 'as found' respectable subjects. Golden Lane's unbuilt streets-in-the-air haunted British housing for two decades before the Smithsons finally built the idea at Robin Hood Gardens, with famously contested results — demolition began in 2017, and a three-story chunk was salvaged for the V&A. The Economist cluster remains their most admired work, a lesson in how towers might behave politely in St James's. Alison died in 1993, Peter in 2003; their influence, as they might have noted with satisfaction, exceeds their built area by orders of magnitude.

projects.title: Hunstanton School
projects.blurb: A Miesian steel frame with its services, brick and bones all left showing — the building that named the New Brutalism.

projects.title: Economist Building
projects.blurb: Three Portland-stone towers of graded height around a raised plaza off St James's Street; their masterclass in urban manners.

projects.title: Robin Hood Gardens
projects.blurb: Streets-in-the-air finally built as two concrete slabs around a green mound; argued over for decades, demolished from 2017, fragment saved by the V&A.

projects.title: Upper Lawn Pavilion
projects.blurb: Their own weekend solar pavilion on an old cottage wall — a two-decade experiment in camping inside architecture.

projects.title: House of the Future
projects.blurb: A full-scale plastic dwelling for the Ideal Home Exhibition, complete with costumed inhabitants and a self-rinsing bath; pop before pop.

projects.title: Golden Lane Housing
projects.blurb: The competition entry whose photomontaged street decks — Marilyn Monroe included — reprogrammed a generation of British housing.

projects.title: Sugden House
projects.blurb: An ordinary-looking brick house made strange by exact placement of every window; the 'as found' applied to suburbia.

projects.title: Garden Building, St Hilda's College
projects.blurb: A square student residence wrapped in a timber lattice, rooms turned to the trees — their gentlest built work.

projects.title: Hexenhaus
projects.blurb: Two decades of delicate timber additions to a client's cottage in a German forest, including a porch for his cat.

projects.title: Berlin Hauptstadt
projects.blurb: A competition plan carpeting central Berlin with a raised pedestrian net over the traffic — the mat-city idea in embryo.
